To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) offspring are reasonably reliable reporters of parental CP history but are likely to overestimate the prevalence of CP in their parents and are less reliable when asked to specify the specific locations of parental pain; (2) the relationship between offspring‐reported family pain history and personal pain history is not likely to be mediated by social desriability, negative affect or catastrophizing; and (3) the relationship between family pain history, as reported by offspring, and personal pain history may be spurious

offspring reports of parental history of chronic (pain) conditions are relatively sensitive, but not very specific, and that these reports are moderately reliable, and that offspring‐reported parental pain histories do not appear to be valid predictors of offspring personal chronic pain experience.

(1) Offspring reports of parental CP were moderately reliable, but tended to overestimate the prevalence of CP in both mothers and fathers; (2) Offspring‐reported maternal and paternal CP were associated with offspring reports of having personally experienced chronic pain, but confirmed parental reports of maternal and paternal CP failed to predict offspring reports of personal chronic pain; (3) These results raise questions about the validity of previous reports of relationships between family history of chronic pain and individuals' own experiences of chronic pain
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accuracy of offspring‐reported parental CP histories, and the implications of these findings for the validity of previous research on the role of family history in the etiology of CP.
the reliability of reports of parental history of chronic musculoskeletal pain (MP) provided by adult children.
the relationship between parental chronic pain (CP; defined as pain lasting greater than 6 months) and offspring CP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the offspring's report of parental chronic pain is a valid and reliable method for obtaining information about parental chronic pain.
the offspring‐reported data is not reliable enough for the purposes of this study and therefore cannot be used to support the hypothesis that parental CP is related to offsprings' CP.
the offspring‐reported data are not reliable, but the parent‐reported data are reliable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
offspring are reasonably reliable reporters of whether or not their parents have experienced chronic pain.

offspring reports of parental history of pain are generally accurate, but not completely reliable, and that offspring reports of their own pain are more likely to be affected by their perceptions of parental pain.
offspring‐reported parental CP histories are relatively reliable but not completely accurate, and may be more accurate than confirmed parental reports.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the accuracy of offspring‐reported parental CP histories may be limited.
the reliability of offspring‐reported parental chronic pain history is relatively modest and should be interpreted with caution.
the offspring‐reported family history of chronic pain is not a good proxy for a confirmed family history.
